conceptTag: Lead a team through a merger
readerTitle: Two crews, one team: your first month after a merger
caseNote: 가상 사례 (배관·난방 수리 회사 합병, 급여 대행 B2B 회사 합병) · 통계나 실제 기업 사례 없음
insight: 합병을 이끄는 일은 새 조직도를 발표하는 일이 아니라, 사람들의 '나는 어떻게 되나' 질문에 먼저 답하고 권한 밖의 사람들을 변화의 공동 주인으로 만드는 일이다.
misconception: 합병은 위에서 결정된 일이니 새 방식을 빨리, 확실하게 지시하면 팀은 따라온다.

sources.text: PIXO 유닛 PPL-07 개념 레슨: Leading change (PPL-07-03), Influence without authority (PPL-07-04)

factChecks.note: 이 레슨에는 합병 실패율 같은 통계를 일부러 넣지 않았습니다. 편집 과정에서 수치를 추가하지 마세요. 추가한다면 1차 출처가 필요합니다.
PPL-07-03, PPL-07-04 개념 레슨의 용어와 정의(예: 이유 설명, 작은 성과, 상대가 중요하게 여기는 것 찾기)와 표현이 일치하는지 게시 전 대조하세요.
회사 이름(Rivera Plumbing, North Heat)은 가상입니다. 실제 동명 업체가 있는지 확인하고, 있으면 이름을 바꾸세요.

cards.title: Two crews, one team: your first month after a merger
body: On Friday, Rivera Plumbing bought North Heat. On Monday, you lead 14 technicians: seven in red shirts, seven in blue.
Nobody has quit yet. But the break room has gone quiet, and two blue-shirt techs are asking about pay at a rival firm.

image.label: Two groups of technicians standing apart in one break room
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 한 휴게실에 빨간 작업복 기술자 무리와 파란 작업복 무리가 서로 떨어져 서 있음. 가운데 커피머신 앞에 리더 한 명. 분위기는 어색하지만 적대적이지 않게. 실제 회사 로고나 상표 없음.

cards.title: What do you do in week one?
body: The owners have decided some things: one company name, one pay scale by year-end. Many things aren't decided yet, like which scheduling system to keep.
How do you open?

options.text: Announce the full new process on day one, so there's no confusion
options.feedback: You gain speed but skip the why. **Leading change** starts with reasons people can accept, and half your team has none yet.

options.text: Say nothing until every detail is final
options.feedback: You avoid promising things you can't keep. But silence gets filled with rumors, and the rumors are usually worse than the truth.

options.text: Meet both crews: share what's decided, what isn't, and when they'll know. Ask what they fear losing
options.feedback: This is **leading change** at work: honest about the unknowns, clear on timing, and listening before deciding.

cards.title: People ask "me" questions first.
body: In a merger, people don't start with the strategy. They start with: Will I keep my job? My pay? My van? My boss?
Until those questions get answers, or at least honest dates, people can't hear anything else. Your growth plan sounds like noise.
So in your first meeting, the blue-shirt crew learns that pay stays the same until year-end, and that a new pay scale comes in November. It's not everything. It's enough to stop the job hunting.

cards.title: Explain why, protect what matters, win early.
body: Leading change means giving people a reason, showing what won't change, and getting an early win they can see.

For your crews: both firms' warranties stay honored. North Heat's habit of calling customers after each job becomes standard for everyone. And the scheduling system gets picked after both crews test both options for two weeks.
Each blue-shirt tech now sees something of theirs survive. That's what makes the rest of the change bearable.

image.label: A merged checklist with items from both companies
image.brief: 한 장의 체크리스트 인포그래픽. 항목마다 빨간 점 또는 파란 점으로 출처 표시: "Both warranties honored"(빨강+파랑), "Follow-up call after every job"(파랑), "Scheduling system: test both"(빨강+파랑). 두 색이 고르게 섞인 느낌. 로고 없음.

cards.title: Dana won't use the new job app.
body: Dana is North Heat's most senior tech. She doesn't report to you; she works for the service director. Her crew follows her lead. She calls the new job-ticket app "Rivera's toy" and keeps writing paper tickets.
What do you do?

options.text: Ask the owner to order her to use it
options.feedback: You may get grudging use. You also prove the blue shirts lost, and Dana's crew follows her resentment, not the order.

options.text: Show her data on how much faster billing is with the app
options.feedback: Good reasons help. But they answer your concern, not hers, so they rarely move someone who feels her crew is being erased.

options.text: Ask what she worries about, then invite her to shape the rollout and train her crew
options.feedback: **Influence without authority**: find what she values, give her a real role, and her standing works for the change.

cards.eyebrow: Concept at work · Influence without authority
cards.title: Trade on what the other person cares about.
body: When you can't order someone, you find what they value and offer it. Dana cares about her crew's reputation for careful work.
It turns out the app has no field for her crew's safety checklist. She adds it. The app gets better, she trains her crew, and her name is on the version everyone uses.
She hasn't been beaten. She's been given credit. That's why her crew follows.

cards.title: Don't promise what isn't yours to promise.
body: Under pressure, leaders say "No one will lose their job." If the owners later cut roles, every honest thing you said gets thrown out with that promise.
Involving people also has limits. Dana shapes the rollout; she doesn't get a veto. Make the line clear early, or co-design turns into endless delay.
cards.softwareNote: After a software acquisition, the same fights happen over which codebase, tools or ticket system wins. Letting respected engineers from both teams set the test criteria usually beats a top-down pick.

cards.title: Now it's a payroll services firm.
body: Your firm runs payroll for small businesses and just merged with a rival. You lead client services for both teams. You must move everyone to one client process within a quarter. The acquired team is anxious, and its most trusted account manager sits in sales, outside your team.
Which plan?

options.text: Email the new process with a firm deadline
options.feedback: It's fast and clear. But with no reason and no allies, people comply on paper and clients feel the anxiety.

options.text: Pilot with one account manager from each firm and a few clients, ask the trusted sales colleague to help, share the early win, then roll out
options.feedback: This combines **leading change** (an early, visible win) with **influence without authority** (a respected ally outside your team).

options.text: Keep both processes for a year until things settle
options.feedback: It buys calm now. But two ways of working harden into two cultures, and the change gets harder later.

cards.title: Answer the "me" questions, then make others co-owners.
body: You used **leading change**: honest answers, visible keepsakes, early wins. You used **influence without authority**: finding what people outside your control care about and giving them a real role.
**Try it today:** pick one change you're leading. Name one person you can't instruct who could make or break it. Write down what they care about most.
